Name It And Claim It
name it and KLAME it
slogan (verb phrase)
A rhyming catchphrase of the twentieth-century Word-of-Faith movement (E. W. Kenyon, Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland), sometimes mocked even by its own adherents as 'name it and claim it' or 'blab it and grab it.' The formula: name the thing desired — healing, wealth, a spouse, a parking space — and claim it as already yours by a 'word of faith,' on the premise that faith is a force that compels God to deliver.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
Word-of-Faith presumption that commands God instead of beseeching Him; biblical prayer asks 'according to his will' and bows, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt.'

📖 Biblical Definition

Biblical prayer is petition offered to a sovereign God in submission to His will, never a technique for commanding Him. The pattern is fixed in Gethsemane, where the Son Himself prayed, 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39). The apostle frames all confident asking the same way: 'if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us' (1 John 5:14) — the confidence is real, but it is bounded by His will, not ours. So James rebukes the presumption that schedules God's hand: 'ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that' (James 4:15). Faith in Scripture is not a force we wield over God but trust we place in God; its posture is the empty open hand of a beggar, not the closed fist of a creditor. We name our requests; God, not our naming, decides.

📜 Origin & Era

A Word-of-Faith formula treating faith as a force that compels God to deliver what one 'claims'; rebutted by Gethsemane's 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39) and asking 'according to his will' (1 John 5:14).

NAME IT AND CLAIM IT, slogan. A Word-of-Faith formula: name a desired thing and claim it as already granted by a 'word of faith.'

Source: the Word-of-Faith / Positive Confession movement (Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland); also mocked as 'blab it and grab it.'

Premise: faith is a spiritual force or law that, rightly applied, obligates God to deliver health and wealth.

Rebutted by Matt. 26:39 ('not as I will, but as thou wilt') and 1 John 5:14 (asking 'according to his will') — petition in submission, not command.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 26:39 — "And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."

1 John 5:14 — "And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:"

James 4:15 — "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that."

Job 42:2 — "I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee."

Psalm 115:3 — "But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

James 4:3 — "Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Word-of-Faith presumption turns prayer into a technique that commands God, treating faith as a force that obligates Him to deliver; Scripture answers that we ask 'according to his will' and bow, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt.'

expand to see more

The corruption inverts the creature and the Creator. In Scripture God is sovereign and man is a suppliant; 'name it and claim it' reverses the order, casting the believer as the one who decrees and God as the one obligated to perform. The Word-of-Faith teachers make this explicit: faith is reclassified as an impersonal 'force' or 'spiritual law' that operates by fixed principle, so that a confession spoken in sufficient faith must produce its object, and God Himself is bound by the law of faith He supposedly set in motion. This is not the God of the Bible, who 'hath done whatsoever he hath pleased' (Ps. 115:3) and whose counsel no man may withhold (Job 42:2). It is a domesticated deity, a vending machine that dispenses on the insertion of the right coin of confession. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the Word-of-Faith claim is named here to rebut it.

The doctrine also wounds the very souls it courts. When the named thing does not come — when the cancer is not healed, the bankruptcy not averted, the spouse not given — the system has only one explanation: the sufferer did not have enough faith, or spoke a stray word of doubt that 'cancelled' the claim. So affliction is compounded with guilt, and the sick are taught to blame themselves for a sovereignty that was never theirs to command. Scripture knows a holier sorrow: Paul prayed thrice that his thorn depart, and the answer was not a granted claim but a sufficient grace — 'My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness' (2 Cor. 12:9). The apostle did not 'claim' his healing; he received his God.

The recovery is the prayer the Lord Himself prayed and taught. He taught us to ask, 'Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven' (Matt. 6:10), and He prayed in the garden, with the cup of wrath before Him, 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39). That is the spine of all faithful prayer: bold to ask anything, humble to surrender everything, certain only that He 'doeth all things well' (Mark 7:37). The confidence of 1 John 5:14 is not the confidence of a man who has compelled God but of a child who trusts a Father — we ask 'according to his will,' and rest in it whether He grants or withholds.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A Word-of-Faith rhyme casting faith as a force that obligates God; Scripture makes prayer petition in submission — 'according to his will' (1 John 5:14), 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matt. 26:39).

expand to see more

English: a Word-of-Faith catchphrase (Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland); 'name' the desire, 'claim' it as granted by confession.

Greek (concept): proseuche, prayer as petition to God — in 1 John 5:14 bounded by 'according to his will' (kata to thelema autou).

Biblical posture: Matt. 26:39, the Son's 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' — the open hand of a suppliant, not the closed fist of a creditor.

Usage

"They told her to 'name it and claim it,' and when the healing did not come they told her she had not believed — affliction crowned with guilt."

"The Son in the garden did not claim the cup away; He prayed 'not as I will, but as thou wilt,' and that is the spine of all true prayer."

"Faith is not a force we wield over God but trust we place in God; we name the request and leave the granting to Him."
